newsitem.title: USA: New York environmental bond proposal sparks fight.
newsitem.headline: New York environmental bond proposal sparks fight.

text.p: A fight began developing over the $1.75 billion environmental bond act proposed by New York's Republican Gov. George Pataki, as a key member of the Assembly said he preferred a "pay-as-you-go" approach.

Assembly Majority Leader Michael Bragman supports the projects that would be funded by the act but believes the measure imposes too much debt and would not create long-term jobs, a spokesman for the Syracuse Democrat said.

Bragman spokesman, Darren Dorp noted that the cost of the bond act to fund a cleanup of state air, land and water, rises to nearly $3 billion when the cost of about $1.1 billion of debt service over 40 years is included.

He said Bragman wants to pay for the environmental projects each year by using the funds that otherwise would be used to repay the debt. He noted that New York has one of the nation's lowest bond ratings and one of the highest debt levels.
"Going with pay-as-you-go would not give you that huge lump sum, but it does give you a steady stream of income...and avoid borrowing costs," Dorp said.
The bond act, which goes to the voters in November, would set aside about $100 million a year from the retail transfer tax to repay the debt.

Bragman's spokesman added the state likely would only benefit economically from a temporary surge in hirings to clean up the polluted areas, which range from abandoned industrial sites in cities to Long Island Sound.

A campaign spokesman for Pataki, Gary Sheffer, disputed Bragman's concerns about the impact of the additional borrowing on the state's finances. "(The act) is a fiscally sound, targeted approach to our most pressing environmental problems."

Sheffer added that the pay-as-you-go approach risks increasing the final bill by delaying important cleanup projects that will become more costly over time, and disagreed with Bragman's assessment of the economic benefits the act offers.
This position was echoed by one of a number of environmental groups that supports the envirnomental bond act.

Paul Elston, chairman of the New York League of Conservation Voters, in prepared remarks said "This is an act of supreme fiscal responsibility. One of the things you do when you run a successful business is raise money to make capital investments that will save you money in the future."
The League is coordinating the coalition of environmental groups.

Further, the campaign official reiterated Pataki's statements that purifying the state's air, land and water will make it more competitive, and create more jobs. For example, once industrial sites are cleaned up, they can be reused by other companies.

The Pataki campaign spokesman noted that Bragman represents an area that borders Lake Onondaga. The Pataki Administration has called this body of water one of the most polluted in the country, a label Bragman's spokesman did not dispute..
